title: Coin values
keyIdea: Each coin and note has a value, written as a number on it. The coins are 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2, and the notes start at £5 and £10. The number tells you what it is worth, not the size: the big 2p is worth less than the small 5p. One coin can be worth the same as lots of smaller coins, and £1 is one pound, which is 100 pence.
familyTip: Tip a purse of coins onto the table. Ask your child to find each coin by its number, colour and shape, then line them up from least to most. Hold up a 2p and a 5p and ask which buys more. Play shop with toys priced 1p to 10p and swap one 10p for ten 1p coins.

visual.caption: Worth less than 10p, or 10p or more? Drag each coin, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find each coin, pick the coin worth more when size tricks you, line coins up from least to most, swap one coin for small coins, check a robot.

kid: We pay with coins and notes. Each one has a number on it. The number tells you how much it is worth.
The coins are 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2. The p means pence. The £ sign means pounds. Notes are paper money, like a £5 note and a £10 note.
Big does not mean more. The 2p is a big coin, but the 5p is worth more, because 5 is more than 2. Look at the number, not the size.
One coin can be worth the same as lots of coins. One 10p is the same as ten 1p coins. £1 is one pound. That is 100 pence, so it is worth more than 50p.
adult: Ages 5 to 6. England's Year 1 maths asks children to recognise and know the value of different coins and notes. Key words: coin, note, value, worth, penny, pence (p), pound (£), more, less.

Children learn to name each coin from its number, colour and shape: the 1p and 2p are copper, the 5p and 10p are round and silver, the 20p and 50p are silver with seven flat sides, and the £1 (12 sides) and £2 have two colours. They order coins by value and see that one coin can be swapped for several smaller ones of the same value.

A common mistake is to think a bigger coin is worth more. The 2p is wider than the 5p, the 10p than the 20p, and the 50p than the £1. Another is to think more coins always means more money. Children also read £1 as just 1 and say it is less than 50p. Ask what the number says, and swap coins with real money so they see equal values.

In the lab your child finds coins by their number, picks the coin worth more in pairs where the bigger coin is worth less, taps coins into order from least to most, fills a tray with small coins until it matches one coin, and checks a robot that says the 2p is worth more than the 5p.

practice.hint: Each 1p coin is worth one penny. Count in 1s.
practice.explain: Each 1p is worth 1p, so {a} of them make {a}p.

practice.prompt: Sam has {a} coins. Each one is a 2p. How many pence does he have?
practice.hint: Each 2p is worth 2 pence. Count in 2s.
practice.explain: Count in 2s, once for each coin: {a} lots of 2p make {=2*a}p.

practice.prompt: Which coin is worth more: the 2p or the 5p?
practice.hint: Look at the numbers on the coins, not the size.
practice.explain: 5 is more than 2, so the 5p is worth more, even though the 2p coin is bigger.

practice.hint: The 20p and 50p are silver coins with flat sides.
practice.explain: The 20p and the 50p both have 7 flat sides. The 1p and £2 are round.

practice.prompt: Ava has one 50p coin. Ben has three 1p coins. Who has more money?
practice.hint: Add up what the coins are worth, not how many coins.
practice.explain: Ava has 50p. Ben has 1p + 1p + 1p = 3p. One coin can be worth more than three.

pool.prompt: How many 1p coins make the same as one {a}p coin?
pool.hint: A coin worth {a}p is worth {a} pennies.
pool.explain: Each 1p is one penny, so {a} of them are worth the same as one {a}p coin.

pool.hint: Count in 10s: 10, 20, 30 and so on. How many 10s did you say?
pool.explain: Counting in 10s up to {=10*a} takes {a} jumps, so {a} 10p coins make {=10*a}p.

pool.hint: £1 is one pound. How many pence is one pound?
pool.explain: £1 is one pound, which is 100 pence. 100p is more than 50p, so £1 is worth more.

pool.hint: Find the smallest number of pence.
pool.explain: The 1p is worth one penny: the least of any coin.

pool.hint: Notes are paper money. Coins are metal.
pool.explain: A £5 note is paper money. It is worth more than any coin, even the £2.

pool.prompt: The 10p coin is bigger than the 20p coin. Which is worth more?
pool.hint: Size can trick you. Look at the number.
pool.explain: 20 is more than 10, so the 20p is worth more, even though the 10p coin is bigger.

pool.prompt: Which order goes from least to most?
pool.explain: 2 is less than 5, and 5 is less than 20, so the order is 2p, 5p, 20p.

pool.hint: Only two coins are brown: the smallest values.
pool.explain: The 1p and 2p are copper coloured. The 10p and 50p are silver.
